name: Firmus Grid Limited, trading as Firmus Technologies (ACN 638 040 534)
headquarters: Sydney, NSW, Australia (Level 14, 333 George Street); operations base in Launceston, Tasmania
employees: Not disclosed; the company says the Benmax acquisition will 'more than double' its global workforce to 340 (Aug 2026)

ownership.notes: Unlisted as of 26 Sep 2026: no ASX record, no ASX upcoming-float entry and no lodged prospectus. The company calls itself Firmus Grid Limited in releases since March 2026 (ABN Lookup still shows Firmus Grid Pty Ltd, ACN 638 040 534, main business location Sydney from 1 Sep 2026). A Reuters-reported term sheet (21 Sep 2026) times an ASX IPO of about A$7B: bookbuild 6-7 Oct, prospectus 8 Oct, listing 22 Oct 2026, with founders' shares 10% released after one year and a further 39.9% after two. Named shareholders include Coatue, NVIDIA, Blackstone vehicles, Jane Street, Ellerston Capital and Maas Group (~3.2% fully diluted); investor preference shares convert one-for-one into ordinary shares (Maas Group filing).

summary: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: Firmus is an Australian neocloud that develops, owns and operates its own AI factories and sells dedicated NVIDIA capacity from them. It says contracted customer capacity passed 900 MW on 8 Sep 2026, with OpenAI signed as anchor customer for two Malaysian sites that are not yet built. Against that it has two operating sites (Melbourne, inside a CDC Data Centres facility, and Singapore) and five under development. It is also a direct buyer of its own power chain, but in Australia that door is contracted away: Maas Group's JLE is 'the exclusive supplier of power train units for Firmus' Australian pipeline' (Maas ASX filing, A$855M order, 4 Aug 2026). What Firmus still buys itself is its connection substations, UPS and batteries (on Eaton's EnergyAware platform), backup generators and a behind-the-meter battery trial at Wesley Vale. BACKGROUND: Incorporated in Australia in 2019 and run from Launceston until its 2026 move to Sydney. Press traces its origin to bitcoin mining. Its first cloud brand, Sustainable Metal Cloud (SMC), launched in Singapore in 2023 on immersion-cooled 'HyperCube' modules; the current generation is direct-to-chip liquid cooled for GB300 and Vera Rubin. Equity: A$330M (Sep 2025, NVIDIA joining), A$500M (Nov 2025), US$505M (Apr 2026, US$5.5B post-money) and US$2B (Aug 2026, above US$10.5B post-money), plus a US$10B Blackstone-led debt facility (Feb 2026). No revenue figure has ever been published. Reuters (24 Sep 2026, citing two people familiar with a draft prospectus) reports an expected pro-forma loss after tax of '$77 million' for the half-year to 31 Dec 2026, ahead of an ASX IPO the term sheet times for 22 Oct 2026. SemiAnalysis rates it Silver in ClusterMAX 3.0 (23 Sep 2026).
ecosystemRole: We assess Firmus as the corpus's first Asia-Pacific neocloud and its clearest case of a neocloud that is also the buyer of its own power chain. Basis: its South Australian campuses are 'owned and operated by Firmus', and it says it is 'building and paying for our own connection substations up front'. It issues the purchase orders for modular 'Firmus Power Cube' power trains and high-voltage infrastructure (Maas Group's ASX filings). It runs UPS and batteries through its Synert subsidiary on Eaton's EnergyAware platform. It contracts firming, not batteries, through a 12-year, 600 MW Gunvor supply deal that underwrites 1.5 GWh of third-party storage by 2032. For a power-equipment seller the Australian power train is locked by JLE's exclusivity, which Maas says covers a 3.3 GW pipeline, so the open doors are elsewhere: tier-2 components inside JLE's Power Cubes, UPS and batteries, behind-the-meter storage (the Wesley Vale R&D factory), and the Batam and Malaysian sites, built with DayOne, which the Australian exclusivity does not reach.

productsAndServices.name: Firmus AI Cloud (formerly Sustainable Metal Cloud) — GPU cloud and dedicated capacity
productsAndServices.description: Firmus sells AI compute from the factories it builds: on-demand and reserved GPU instances, bare-metal clusters and multi-year dedicated capacity contracts. The catalogue lists NVIDIA H200, H100, A100 and L40S 8-GPU nodes, with 'NVIDIA GB300 and Vera Rubin NVL72 – coming soon', WEKA parallel storage, Managed Slurm, CUDA stacks, NIM inference APIs and a PaaS layer via Rafay. It is an NVIDIA Cloud Partner and lists on NVIDIA DGX Cloud Lepton. The cloud began in Singapore in 2023 as Sustainable Metal Cloud (SMC), a venture into which ST Telemedia Global Data Centres made 'a significant investment'; smc.co is held by Firmus Metal International Pte Ltd and the brand is now legacy.
highlights: More than 900 MW of contracted customer capacity 'across all customers' (8 Sep 2026), up from 155 MW in April per Lowyat; no per-customer or per-site breakdown is published

Named customers: OpenAI (anchor, two Malaysian sites, Vera Rubin NVL72), an unnamed 'leading global technology company' (~18,400 GB300 at Melbourne, 'multi-billion dollar'), Fireworks (GB300 and Vera Rubin, Aug 2026) and AI Singapore (256 H200). Reuters reports the draft prospectus names Nvidia, Meta and OpenAI as customers; Firmus has not named Meta

SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX: Silver in 1.0 (Mar 2025), 2.0 (Nov 2025) and 3.0 (23 Sep 2026); the 3.0 test of a development GB300 cluster recorded network drops that killed jobs, a NIC lost in a reboot and 0.25 Gb/s WAN
MLPerf Training v4.0 (Jun 2024): the first published power results — GPT-3 175B on 512 H100 used 468 kWh, at a Singapore facility PUE of 1.10 (company)
productsAndServices.positioning: Sells capacity rather than space: Forbes Australia contrasts it with AirTrunk because 'it supplies customers with access to Nvidia chips rather than requiring them to bring their own'. Press compares it with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN; SemiAnalysis calls it 'our favorite in Asia-Pacific' but places it below CoreWeave and Nebius (Platinum) and Oracle and Google Cloud (Gold)
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Direct multi-year capacity contracts with labs and hyperscale platforms; on-demand cloud; NVIDIA DGX Cloud Lepton marketplace
targetSegments: frontier AI labs and AI-native companies
sovereign and research customers in Australia and Southeast Asia
productsAndServices.roadmap: GB300 and Vera Rubin NVL72 capacity 'coming soon'; five sites targeting ready-for-service 'over the next 24 months' (from Sep 2026); an 'Australian AI Access Program' for researchers that it 'intends to establish'

productsAndServices.name: HyperCube modular AI factory
productsAndServices.description: The HyperCube is Firmus's trademarked building block: 'each HyperCube is a physical module of the AI Factory, designed to house 32 NVL racks in a primarily liquid-cooled, high-density configuration'. It 'integrates advanced liquid cooling, mechanical systems and electrification into a repeatable infrastructure system manufactured and prefabricated in regional New South Wales' and is co-designed to NVIDIA DSX blueprints. The 2023 generation was 'multiple modularised 1MW HyperCubes' on single-phase immersion cooling; the current generation uses direct-to-chip liquid cooling for GB300 and Vera Rubin, with closed-loop propylene-glycol circuits and dry coolers. Benmax fabricates the mechanical and cooling modules in Queanbeyan, NSW; Firmus agreed on 13 Aug 2026 to buy Benmax's Fabrication, Design and Projects businesses for A$300M.
highlights: PUE 1.1 claimed on the infrastructure page; the energy policy targets PUE of 1.15 or less against a NABERS 5-star benchmark of 1.40
'Rack-level electrical with CDU-fed systems and no PDU overhead'; the company claims about 15% less power loss per megawatt
'UPS systems engineered to deliver FCAS, load modulation, and firming capacity'
Six patents covering 'thermal systems, silicon-aware orchestration, and power integration'
The domestic supply chain is sized for 'up to 1.5GW of AI facility delivery per year', with more than A$300M committed (Feb 2026)
productsAndServices.positioning: 'No colocation, no containers. Full-stack infrastructure' (company). SemiAnalysis (ClusterMAX 2.0) judged 'the bulk of Firmus's experience with immersion cooling is misguided, and now wasted' as the platform moved to direct-to-chip cooling
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Internal — built into Firmus-operated factories; adapted into a third-party shell at CDC's Melbourne facility; to be integrated into DayOne-built projects in Southeast Asia
productsAndServices.roadmap: Benmax completion was 'expected between the end of August and the end of September 2026, subject to customary conditions' (Benmax); no completion notice found by 26 Sep 2026. On completion Benmax's managing director Scott Polsen becomes Chief Development Officer

productsAndServices.name: Firmus Power Cube and high-voltage infrastructure (built by JLE, Maas Group)
productsAndServices.description: The electrical content of a Firmus factory is a modular power train called the Firmus Power Cube, designed under the Firmus name and manufactured by JLE Manufacturing & Hire, a subsidiary of Maas Group Holdings (ASX: MGH). Maas's filings describe a Master Services Agreement that 'provides for JLE to be the exclusive supplier of power train units for Firmus' Australian pipeline', an A$200M order for 'modular Power Cubes and associated electrical scope for Firmus' 100MW Launceston AI Factory', and an A$855M work order (4 Aug 2026) for 'the manufacture, supply and delivery of modular Firmus Power Cube solutions and associated high-voltage infrastructure' over 18 months. JLE's stated scope runs from grid connection, high-voltage substation and switchyard, custom transformers and switchgear through to backup power and standby generation.
highlights: Maas benchmarks the business at 'approximately A$200 million of revenue per 100MW of deployed capacity' — about A$2M per MW for the electrical power train
Maas calls it an 'exclusive electrical delivery partnership' for Firmus's 'broader 3.3GW Australian AI Factory portfolio'
Maas reported about A$1.2B of secured electrical work in hand (AGM, 24 Sep 2026); JLE manufactures in Newcastle, Orange and Vietnam
Related party: Maas holds about 3.2% of Firmus (A$410M invested), and 'an entity associated with MGH CEO Wes Maas separately holds a material investment in Firmus'
productsAndServices.positioning: No competing power-train vendor is named for any Australian site; the exclusivity is stated for the Australian pipeline only
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Firmus places purchase orders with JLE under the Master Services Agreement; JLE sources the components
productsAndServices.roadmap: A$855M order to be delivered over 18 months from August 2026; Launceston more than 40% complete at 30 Jun 2026 with delivery in the half to December 2026 (Maas)

productsAndServices.name: Project Southgate and the AI factory campuses
productsAndServices.description: Firmus develops its own campuses. Project Southgate is the Australian programme, targeting 'up to 1.6 gigawatts through 2028' and 'A$73.3 billion' at full scale (Oct 2025); Maas refers to a 3.3 GW Australian pipeline. The flagship is Launceston, Tasmania, with '84MW Critical IT Load' and about 36,800 GB300 due in late 2026. Bell Bay, a former pulp-mill site, has a maximum demand of 288 MW and was approved 6-1 by George Town Council on 25 Aug 2026. Wesley Vale is planned at 26 MW rising to about 52 MW, next to a separate 26 MW R&D factory. Melbourne sits inside a CDC Data Centres facility with about 18,400 GB300 for a global technology customer. In South Australia, Tailem Bend (about 1.0 GW IT) and Stirling North (about 1.3 GW IT) are 'owned and operated by Firmus'. Abroad: Batam, Indonesia, up to 360 MW and 170,000 NVIDIA GPUs with DayOne; two Malaysian sites for OpenAI; and two Singapore sites (Loyang, retrofitted from an STT facility, and Media Hub).
highlights: Seven AI factories in four countries; 'Two sites are operational today, in Australia and Singapore, and five are under development' (8 Sep 2026)

Firmus funds and owns its connection infrastructure: 'We are building and paying for our own connection substations up front'; Bell Bay's plans include 'electrical substations (that Firmus will own)' and a switching station
Backup generation: Wesley Vale 'will have 40 backup generators'; ABC reports Bell Bay's application covers 276 diesel generators, which Firmus first reported as 128
Batam: 'Firmus expects to receive between US$25 and US$30 billion from committed offtake agreements during the first six years' (company, Jun 2026)
productsAndServices.positioning: Power-first siting in Tasmania (hydro) and South Australia (firmed renewables); Firmus says it builds 'from the chip to the grid'
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Capacity sold through the AI Cloud business; campuses are not leased to other operators
productsAndServices.roadmap: Launceston complete late 2026; South Australian supply from mid-2027; Batam GPU deliveries 2027-28; the Hydro Tasmania decision on a 450 MW long-term request expected by the end of 2026 (ABC)

productsAndServices.name: Energy, grid and connectivity platform — Synert, Model-to-Grid, Gunvor supply, subsea cable
productsAndServices.category: Energy procurement, grid services and software
productsAndServices.description: Firmus treats energy as part of the product. Synert, a Firmus subsidiary, runs a smart-UPS platform 'built with Eaton's industry-leading EnergyAware UPS platform' that delivers certified fast frequency response into Australia's NEM from a Tasmanian site (Apr 2025). Synert describes its PowerCube as 'a grid-scale battery platform' with 'batteries in shipping containers'. Model-to-Grid and AI FactoryOS are grid-aware orchestration software built on NVIDIA's DSX blueprint, to be coordinated with AEMO. In South Australia a 12-year wholesale agreement with Gunvor supplies 600 MW of firm electricity from mid-2027, under which Gunvor 'is committing to underwrite 1.2 GW of additional renewable generation and 1.5 GWh of new battery storage capacity by 2032' — first GreenPoint Energy's 200 MW / 800 MWh Koolunga battery. Firmus also underwrote the Bernacchi-1 Bass Strait cable and committed about US$300M to SUBCO's APX East trans-Pacific cable.
highlights: Energy policy: suppliers must deliver 'at least 2.5 MWh of new firming capacity for every 1 MW' of Firmus load; up to 220 hours a year of demand response
Tasmania: a three-year, 104 MW retail supply via Aurora Energy on Hydro Tasmania power, ramping from August to November 2026, plus a 450 MW long-term request under assessment (ABC)
Wesley Vale 26 MW R&D factory 'will test whether behind-the-meter battery energy storage… can provide a more flexible… approach to backup energy', with 'Firmus covering all of the costs'
No first-party mention of solid-state transformers, 800 VDC or HVDC anywhere on firmus.co or synert.co
productsAndServices.positioning: Grid-interactive UPS and demand response are sold as a public benefit to win approvals; firming is bought as a contracted service, not as owned batteries
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Internal; FCAS revenue from the grid; supply contracts with retailers
productsAndServices.roadmap: Gunvor supply from mid-2027; Koolunga commercial operation targeted Q1 2028; Bernacchi-1 ready for service Q2 2027; APX East Q4 2028

relationships.scale: joined the A$330M round; followed on in US$505M and US$2B rounds
relationships.note: NVIDIA is Firmus's shareholder, its GPU supplier and, at Batam, its financing partner: the campus is built on NVIDIA's revenue-sharing and credit-support model.
relationships.context:
NVIDIA joined Firmus's A$330M placement in September 2025, which closed at A$1.85B post-money with Ellerston Capital as cornerstone, and followed on in the US$505M (April 2026) and US$2B (August 2026) rounds.

At Batam, Firmus says it will 'procure NVIDIA infrastructure' under a revenue-sharing and credit-support model and expects US$25-30B of offtake over six years. NVIDIA's own blog names Sharon AI and Firmus 'among the first companies to work with NVIDIA on this new business model'. CDC called NVIDIA the anchor customer of the first Melbourne stage, and the Reuters account of the draft prospectus lists Nvidia among Firmus's customers. Supplier, shareholder, customer and credit backstop at once.

relationships.via: dedicated compute on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 at two Malaysian sites
relationships.note: OpenAI signed a multi-year strategic partnership to contract dedicated AI compute from two Firmus AI factory sites in Malaysia and 'will become an anchor customer of Firmus'.
relationships.context:
Announced by Firmus on 8 Sep 2026, with a quote from Sachin Katti, OpenAI's VP of Compute Strategy. No OpenAI-hosted release was found, and openai.com was unreachable from this session.

The sites are new and not yet built. Their location, MW and any Malaysian partner are undisclosed; Firmus declined to disclose financial terms (Reuters). DayOne is Firmus's named Southeast Asian build partner in general, but is not named for Malaysia.

relationships.note: Firmus's Synert subsidiary runs a smart-UPS grid-services platform 'built with Eaton's industry-leading EnergyAware UPS platform' at a Tasmanian site.
relationships.context: The platform delivers certified fast frequency response into Australia's National Electricity Market from UPS batteries. Firmus's timeline dates first deployment to Q1 2024 ('Synert deployed with Eaton in Tasmania'); the joint showcase release is dated April 2025. Whether Eaton supplies UPS for the new Power Cube power trains, which JLE builds, is not stated.

relationships.scale: US$10B debt facility (lead); equity in the US$2B round
relationships.note: Blackstone funds led Firmus's US$10B debt facility in February 2026 and Blackstone Tactical Opportunities joined the US$2B equity round in August 2026.
relationships.context: The facility was 'led by funds managed by Blackstone Tactical Opportunities, Blackstone Credit & Insurance, and affiliated funds', supported by Coatue, to fund the next phase of Project Southgate; tenor, pricing and the drawn amount are not disclosed.

relationships.via: servers in the immersion-cooled SMC HyperCubes
relationships.note: Supermicro was named as an OEM partner when Sustainable Metal Cloud launched with ST Telemedia in Singapore in 2023.
relationships.context: ST Telemedia's June 2023 release lists 'OEM partners including Supermicro' for the first immersion-cooled HyperCube deployment at STT GDC's Singapore site. No current server OEM is named for the GB300 and Vera Rubin generation.

relationships.note: The benchmark neocloud the Firmus IPO is measured against; SemiAnalysis rates CoreWeave Platinum and Firmus Silver in ClusterMAX 3.0.
relationships.context: Press compares Firmus's float with CoreWeave's 2025 IPO and places it alongside CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN. The two models differ: CoreWeave leases shells from third-party developers, while Firmus builds and owns its campuses.

relationships.note: IREN is the other Australian-founded AI cloud building in South Australia; SemiAnalysis's September 2026 review contrasts the two.
relationships.context: Capital Brief (24 Sep 2026) reports SemiAnalysis's lead author saying Firmus is 'up for the challenge' while rating IREN 'not recommended'. Both are Australian-founded AI clouds, and press groups them as peers in the run-up to the float.

policyExposure.exposure: Firmus's growth outside Australia runs on US-origin GPUs: Vera Rubin NVL72 for OpenAI in Malaysia and up to 170,000 NVIDIA GPUs at Batam, Indonesia. No Firmus-specific US licence or BIS action is on the record, and Firmus's own channels do not discuss export controls as they apply to Malaysia or Indonesia.
policyExposure.mitigation: 'our customers are contractually required to comply with all applicable laws, including export controls and sanctions… we don't comment on individual customers or customer categories' (Bell Bay webinar)

policyExposure.regime: Malaysia Strategic Trade Permit (US-origin AI chips)
policyExposure.exposure: Malaysia requires a Strategic Trade Permit for the export, transhipment or transit of US-origin high-performance AI chips. Firmus's two OpenAI sites in Malaysia sit inside this regime; the company has made no statement on it.

policyExposure.regime: Commonwealth expectations of data centres and AI infrastructure developers
policyExposure.exposure: Firmus names the Commonwealth Government's March 2026 expectations and says its energy policy 'goes beyond' them. The policy commits it to build and pay for its own connection substations, to require at least 2.5 MWh of new firming per MW of load from suppliers, and to curtail up to 220 hours a year.
policyExposure.mitigation: Energy and Australian Water Stewardship policies published June 2026

policyExposure.regime: Tasmania AI Factory Zone and state energy supply
policyExposure.exposure: The Tasmanian campuses depend on state sponsorship and on Hydro Tasmania. Energy for Bell Bay and Wesley Vale is 'subject to finalisation of energy supply arrangements'. Hydro Tasmania is assessing a 450 MW long-term request, with an outcome expected by the end of 2026. Bell Bay's council approval restricts diesel generators to outages, maintenance and emergencies.

policyExposure.regime: South Australia Crown Sponsorship (Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016)
policyExposure.exposure: Firmus is seeking Crown Sponsorship for the Tailem Bend and Stirling North campuses and is engaging ElectraNet, SA Water and Traditional Owners; neither campus has a planning approval on the record.

financials.commentary: Firmus reports no financial statements publicly. Its financial record is a sequence of funding announcements, Maas Group's related-party disclosures and a Reuters account of an unlodged draft prospectus. Collection gap: revenue, contracted revenue backlog, capex and debt drawn are all unknown until the prospectus is lodged (due 8 Oct 2026 per the term sheet).

strategyRead: (High confidence) We assess that Firmus buys its own power chain but has contracted its Australian power train away, so the Australian door for a power-equipment vendor runs through JLE, not Firmus. Basis: Maas Group's ASX filings describe a Master Services Agreement making JLE 'the exclusive supplier of power train units for Firmus' Australian pipeline'. JLE's stated scope runs from the high-voltage substation, transformers and switchgear to standby generation, and it holds an A$855M order on top of A$200M for Launceston. Maas prices the work at about A$200M per 100 MW, and Maas and its CEO's family hold Firmus equity. Indicator to watch: the prospectus's description of the JLE agreement (term, exclusivity scope, termination) and any power-train award outside Australia.

(High confidence) We assess the 900 MW as a sales figure, not a build figure. Basis: the metric is 'total contracted capacity across all customers' against two operating sites (Melbourne inside CDC's building, and Singapore). The first owned campus, Launceston (84 MW IT), completes in late 2026. Bell Bay and Wesley Vale have no energy contract, with a 450 MW Hydro Tasmania decision due by the end of 2026, and the South Australian supply starts only in mid-2027. Indicator to watch: the prospectus's capacity table and the Hydro Tasmania decision.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that storage reaches Firmus through its retailer and its UPS, not as utility-scale battery purchases — with one exception worth watching. Basis: Gunvor underwrites 1.5 GWh of third-party storage, first GreenPoint's Koolunga battery, and Firmus's policy demands 2.5 MWh of firming per MW from suppliers. Synert runs containerised UPS batteries on Eaton's platform. The Wesley Vale 26 MW R&D factory will test behind-the-meter storage as a replacement for diesel backup, with Firmus paying all costs. Indicator to watch: a named behind-the-meter battery supplier at Wesley Vale.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that Firmus has shown no move toward 800 VDC or solid-state transformers, and that its Vera Rubin sites abroad are where one would first appear. Basis: its stated electrical architecture is 'rack-level electrical with CDU-fed systems and no PDU overhead', and nothing on firmus.co or synert.co mentions SSTs, 800 VDC or HVDC. Its Batam and Malaysian sites are built to NVIDIA DSX blueprints for Vera Rubin NVL72, outside the JLE exclusivity. This judgment is an inference from absence. Indicator to watch: a DC-distribution or SST specification for Batam or Malaysia, or a change in the Power Cube's design.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that NVIDIA's several roles and the listing are one risk, not two. Basis: NVIDIA is shareholder, GPU supplier, customer (CDC called it the Melbourne anchor) and, at Batam, provider of revenue-sharing and credit support. Bloomberg, as relayed, reports about US$10B of financing for Batam chips under discussion before the float. The IPO has slipped twice, and a co-CEO's 2016 conviction is being raised by investors. Indicator to watch: prospectus lodgement on 8 Oct and listing on 22 Oct 2026, or a further delay.
